name: Smellmaxxing

lead: Smellmaxxing means improving how you smell, through hygiene, deodorant, diet or fragrance, on the idea that scent adds to attractiveness. A forum thread has asked whether good smell can compensate for looks.

Most body odour comes from bacteria acting on secretions of apocrine glands, which become active at puberty and are concentrated in the armpits. Genetics, notably the ABCC11 gene, and diet also affect odour. Studies report that women tend to prefer the scent of men whose immune genes differ from their own, and that fruit and vegetable intake was linked to sweat described as more pleasant.

paras: People shower regularly, use deodorant or antiperspirant, wash clothes and bedding, care for oral hygiene and choose a fragrance. Deodorants reduce odour, while antiperspirants block sweat pores temporarily. Results are immediate on application.

No notable harms are documented for ordinary hygiene or fragrance use in the sources reviewed. Studies on scent and attraction are small and do not establish how much scent affects perceived attractiveness.

angle.text: Smellmaxxing manages body scent with hygiene, deodorant and fragrance so you smell fresher and come across as more attractive up close. The effect is immediate; body-odour science describes bacteria, genes and diet as the main contributors.

lead: Smellmaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for optimising how you smell, through fragrance, deodorant, body wash and hygiene, so that scent adds to overall attractiveness. Participants treat scent as the part of presentation others notice at close range: a signature fragrance, layered products and a routine that makes someone come across as well-groomed and mature. [1][2]

Wikipedia describes it as a 2020s, social-media-driven practice that began in looksmaxxing communities and then shifted to fragrances, deodorants and body washes, mainly among adolescent boys on TikTok. Motivations named include seduction, self-expression, popularity and appearing more mature. [1][2]

Reference material on body odour states that the main contribution comes from bacterial activity on skin gland secretions, with diet, sex, health and medication also playing roles. [3] Studies discussed in the same reference report that women tend to prefer the scent of men whose immune genes differ from their own, and that fruit and vegetable intake was linked to sweat described as more pleasant. [3]
infobox: Skin bacteria acting on apocrine secretions

paras: Apocrine glands become active at puberty and produce most compounds that skin flora break down into odour molecules, with Corynebacterium species producing lipases that create smelly acids; different bacteria dominate in men and women.[3]

The ABCC11 gene largely determines underarm odour and earwax type. A non-functional variant reduces body odour in people who carry two copies; it is common in East Asian populations (about 80 to 95 percent) and rare in European and African populations (0 to 3 percent).[3] A 2017 study found that men who ate more fruits and vegetables had sweat rated as more pleasant.[3]

Deodorants reduce odour without reducing sweating, usually with alcohol, antibacterial agents and perfume; antiperspirants, including prescription aluminium chloride types, temporarily block sweat pores.[3]

A 2005 study reported that women tend to prefer the scent of men with immune genes (MHC/HLA) different from their own, and a 2016 study linked HLA to partnership and sexual satisfaction.[3] A 2006 Swedish brain-imaging study found differing responses to putative pheromones in heterosexual and homosexual men and in lesbian women, without establishing cause or effect.[3] A 2012 study showed people can distinguish body odours of different age groups.[3]

Wikipedia lists the core aspects of fragrance use as projection (how far a scent carries), sillage (the trail left while moving) and longevity. Layering means combining perfumes, body products, oils or hair mists, often with a "fragrance wardrobe" of scents for different moods, seasons or occasions, with lighter scents for daytime and stronger ones in the evening. Moisturising first is cited as a tip for making scents last. [1]
Body spray, a lighter and usually cheaper product that doubles as a deodorant, is the entry point for many younger users, and Axe is a well-known brand. [2]

Wikipedia, citing a Piper Sandler survey reported by the New York Times, says teen male fragrance spending rose 26 percent from spring 2023, and citing The Economist says boys averaged about 110 dollars a year on fragrance in 2024, up from 75 in 2023. [1] It reports industry figures that TikTok influenced fragrance purchases for 66 percent of Gen Z consumers, and that the trend increased demand for "dupes" of luxury fragrances. [1][2] Critics noted by the same article point to schools banning fragrance and to concerns about patchouli oil demand and deforestation in Indonesia. [1]

No studies found testing smellmaxxing as a looksmaxxing practice or its effect on perceived attractiveness. Related research on body odour and partner preference is described above and is not specific to the term.

The term appears in forum discussions, including a looksmax.org thread asking whether good smells can make up for looks. [4] Wikipedia says the "-maxx" suffix comes from the incelosphere, citing Wired, and describes the trend as having moved from looksmaxxing communities into mainstream fragrance culture. [1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the topic is raised as a question about whether scent can offset looks. [4]

claims.claim: Good smell can make up for weaker looks.
